screens.title: Correlation-Based and Tournament Predictors
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore how branch prediction moves beyond independent two-bit counters to use correlations, selectors, and small caches so a processor can guess both whether a branch is taken and where it goes. You will learn what a global branch history register records, how the gshare predictor mixes that history with a branch address to index a table, and why tournament predictors combine a local and a global view with a meta-predictor to pick the best source of truth. We also cover the branch target buffer, which supplies destination addresses for taken branches, and the return address stack, which restores return addresses for nested calls. These pieces are practical engineering: gshare and tournament designs appear in real processors because correlated behavior and call/return patterns provide consistent signals that simple per-branch counters miss. By the end you will understand the key trade-offs — accuracy versus aliasing and hardware cost — and you will be ready to extend a branch-prediction simulator to implement gshare, a tournament selector, and a small BTB. Think about a detective who uses a notebook of recent cases: that notebook is the global history that helps make smarter local decisions.

screens.title: Why simple 2-bit predictors fall short
screens.narratorSegment: A simple two-bit saturating counter treats each branch as independent, which works well for some patterns but fails when branches are correlated. Define correlation here as a statistical dependence: the outcome of branch B changes depending on whether a previous branch A was taken. For example, consider code where a second comparison only runs after the first test passes. A 2-bit counter for branch B averages all outcomes it sees and may settle on the majority behavior, losing the conditional nuance. That leads to predictable mistakes when B behaves differently in the two contexts. A concrete case is Branch B taken 90 percent of the time when Branch A was taken but only 30 percent when Branch A was not taken. The 2-bit predictor may converge near 60 percent and mispredict frequently in both contexts. The misconception learners often have is thinking more bits solve correlation; adding bits to a per-branch counter doesn't add context about other branches. The correct remedy is to add history: a register that records recent outcomes, so the predictor can index different table entries per context. The takeaway is simple: independence assumptions are cheap but lose accuracy when program flow carries contextual signals that connect branches.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Independent 2-bit counters miss context: correlated branches need history so different execution contexts map to different predictions.

content.html:
Core Concept Independent vs correlated
Independent 2-bit predictor
Each branch has its own 2-bit saturating counter. No information crosses branches.
  • • Definition: per-branch 2-bit counters track recent taken/not-taken for one branch.
  • • Limitation: averages behavior across contexts and loses conditional patterns.
  • • Misconception: adding bits to the counter captures correlation — it does not.
Key Takeaway

Use history, not larger counters, to capture correlations between branches.

Concrete example
Three branches where the third depends on the first two:
Trace A
If prior pattern is 11 then Branch 3 is taken 90% of the time.
Trace B
If prior pattern is 00 then Branch 3 is taken 30% of the time.
Because a 2-bit counter sees a mixed stream, it converges to an average and mispredicts in each context. A predictor that indexes based on prior bits can separate these contexts and store distinct counters for them.

screens.title: Global Branch History Register (GHR)
screens.narratorSegment: The global branch history register, or GHR, is a compact shift register that records the taken/not-taken outcomes of the most recent N branches. Each bit is 1 for taken and 0 for not taken, so an 8-bit GHR might read 10110101 and represent the last eight outcomes in order. The GHR provides temporal context for the next branch: patterns of recent branches often repeat across program behavior, and these patterns can strongly influence a later branch. A key practical detail is which branches contribute bits — typically all conditional branches update the GHR in fetch or retire stages. A common misconception is that longer GHRs always improve accuracy. Longer history captures longer patterns but increases table aliasing and hardware cost, and older bits might be irrelevant for the current decision. Balance is required: small GHRs capture local correlations with lower aliasing risk. An example: a conditional inside a sequence of checks can be predicted more accurately when the GHR preserves the outcomes of those checks. In practice, the GHR is the contextual notebook the predictor consults before making a decision; understanding what it records and how long it should be is the first step to building correlation-based predictors.

keyIdea.title: GHR Role
keyIdea.text: GHR records recent branch outcomes as context; size choices trade off pattern depth and aliasing/cost.

content.html:
Definition Global Branch History Register
What the GHR stores
An N-bit vector of recent taken (1) and not-taken (0) outcomes, shifting in a new bit each branch.
Example value: 10110101 represents eight recent outcomes. Use this as context when indexing pattern tables so the predictor can distinguish behavior after different histories.
Misconception

Longer history is always better — not necessarily. More bits raise aliasing risk and hardware cost, and older events may not help prediction.

Why it matters
  • • Context separation: Different histories map to distinct table entries and counters.
  • • Captures correlations: When later branches depend on earlier outcomes, history helps.
  • • Hardware trade-offs: Width and update timing affect complexity and latency.

Simulate 8-bit vs 16-bit GHR on a correlated trace and compare prediction accuracy and aliasing counts.

screens.title: Gshare predictor: combining PC and GHR
screens.narratorSegment: Gshare mixes global history with branch-specific information by XORing bits of the program counter with the GHR to produce an index into a table of 2-bit saturating counters. This simple operation distributes contexts so different branches with the same history do not always alias to the same entry. The formula is: Index = (PC XOR GHR) mod TableSize. Practically, implementations often use the lower bits of the PC and the low-order bits of the GHR for the XOR. A common implementation detail is to mask to the table size using bitwise AND when the table size is a power of two. For example, with an 8-bit GHR and a 256-entry table, XOR the low 8 bits of PC with the GHR to get an 8-bit index. A misconception is thinking XOR always eliminates aliasing; XOR reduces some alias patterns but does not remove aliasing entirely. Concrete example: suppose the GHR is 0b11001010 and the PC low bits are 0b10101010; XOR yields 0b01100000 which is used to select a saturating counter. In a simulator, implement this index computation in fetch or prediction stage, update the counter on branch resolution, and update the GHR by shifting in the actual outcome. The result: gshare often raises accuracy for branches whose outcomes depend on recent history.

keyIdea.title: Gshare Formula
keyIdea.text: Index = (PC XOR GHR) mod TableSize; XOR mixes global context and branch identity to reduce aliasing for correlated branches.

content.html:
Process Gshare Indexing
How Gshare computes an index
XOR the low-order bits of the program counter with the GHR, then mask to the table size.
// pseudocode for gshare index
pc_low = PC & (TableSize - 1)
index = (pc_low ^ GHR) & (TableSize - 1)
predict = counter_table[index] >= 2 ? TAKEN : NOT_TAKEN
Update rules: increment or decrement the 2-bit counter at that index on branch resolution, and shift the actual outcome into the GHR.
Concrete walkthrough
With an 8-bit GHR and a 256-entry table, use the 8 low bits of PC. Example: PC low = 10101010, GHR = 11001010, XOR = 01100000; consult counter_table[0x60].
Common mistake: XOR eliminates aliasing — it helps but collisions remain. Measure alias counts in your simulator rather than assuming perfect separation.
Try this
Implement the XOR index and run a correlated trace to compare accuracy with a per-branch 2-bit predictor.

screens.title: PAg vs GAg: per-branch and global pattern tables
screens.narratorSegment: Correlation-based predictors come in multiple flavors and each makes different trade-offs between per-branch specificity and global sharing. PAg uses a per-branch history register for each dynamic branch and then a shared global pattern table that maps those per-branch histories to predictions. That gives per-branch context while still sharing a global prediction table. GAg uses a single global history register and a single global pattern table shared by all branches; it captures global correlations but is more prone to aliasing since unrelated branches map into the same table patterns. The core trade-off is specificity versus sharing: PAg gives more specificity for heavy branches at the cost of more storage for per-branch history, while GAg is simpler and cheaper but can suffer when many branches collide in the same entries. A frequent misconception is that per-branch histories eliminate aliasing; they reduce aliasing for that branch but the global pattern table can still collide entries from different branches. A concrete example: a hot loop branch benefits from a dedicated per-branch history because its short repeating pattern maps cleanly to different pattern table entries than other code. When designing a predictor, measure aliasing and storage cost against accuracy to choose the right balance for your target workload.

keyIdea.title: PAg vs GAg
keyIdea.text: PAg provides per-branch histories with a shared pattern table; GAg shares history and table globally — trade specificity for simplicity.

content.html:
Comparison PAg vs GAg
PAg (per-branch history)
Each branch has its own history register that indexes into a global pattern table.
  • • Strength: captures branch-specific patterns well.
  • • Cost: storage for per-branch history table.
  • • Use case: hot branches with stable local behavior benefit most.
GAg (global history & table)
Single global history and single global pattern table shared by all branches.
  • • Strength: simple and compact to implement.
  • • Weakness: more aliasing when unrelated branches map to same entries.
  • • Use case: workloads where global correlations dominate and storage is tight.
Design choice
Choose PAg for branch-specific fidelity, GAg for compact global correlation capture, or hybrid approaches when both behaviors appear.

screens.title: Tournament predictors and the meta-predictor
screens.narratorSegment: A tournament predictor runs two or more predictors in parallel, typically a local predictor that relies on the branch address and a global predictor that uses GHR, and then uses a meta-predictor or selector to choose which prediction to trust for each branch. The meta-predictor is often implemented as a 2-bit counter per branch index that increments when the global predictor succeeds and decrements when the local predictor succeeds, or vice versa. Over time it favors the predictor that has been more accurate for that branch. This design addresses the central practical observation: different branches have different predictability characteristics — some are best solved by local repetition, others by global correlations. The trade-off is extra hardware: two prediction tables plus the meta-selector. The value shows up in real workloads: tournaments can reach high accuracy because they adapt to branch behavior at the granularity of branch addresses. A concrete example: a loop counter is best handled by a local predictor, while a conditional dependent on a prior branch benefits from the global predictor; the meta-predictor learns which to use. A common misconception is that the meta-predictor instantly switches; in reality it learns gradually from outcomes and can be conservative to avoid thrashing. The takeaway: tournament predictors adaptively pick the right model for each branch and are a key building block of modern high-accuracy predictors.

keyIdea.title: Tournament
keyIdea.text: Run local and global predictors in parallel and use a meta-predictor to learn which one to trust per branch.

content.html:
Core Concept Tournament Predictor
Structure
  • • Local predictor: indexed by branch address, captures stable local patterns.
  • • Global predictor: often gshare, captures inter-branch correlations via GHR.
  • • Meta-predictor: a selector table that learns which predictor was more accurate per branch.
Concrete selector behavior
A 2-bit selector per branch index can count votes. If global was correct, increment; if local was correct, decrement. A strong bias is needed to avoid flip-flopping on noisy branches.
Misconception: tournament predictors are magic — they improve accuracy but cost extra table entries and complexity. The benefit is adaptation: the hardware picks the best predictor for each dynamic branch.
Key Takeaway

Adaptivity beats one-size-fits-all: let hardware learn which predictor to trust for each branch.

screens.title: How a tournament predictor operates at runtime
screens.narratorSegment: At runtime a tournament predictor predicts by running local and global predictors in parallel and using the meta-predictor to pick one result. The process starts at fetch: both predictors compute their choices based on the branch address and the GHR. The meta-predictor provides a selector value that determines which prediction to send to the fetch pipeline. Speculation proceeds; when the branch resolves in execute or retire, the predictor logic compares each predictor's guess to the actual outcome. The meta-predictor is updated: if the chosen predictor was correct and the other was incorrect, the selector is biased toward the chosen predictor; if the other predictor was correct, the selector is adjusted in the opposite direction. The predictors' own tables are updated as usual. A common misconception is thinking the meta-predictor only toggles when the chosen predictor fails; in fact it considers both predictors' correctness and adjusts slowly to avoid oscillation on noisy branches. Concrete example: local predicted taken, global predicted not-taken, actual outcome not-taken — the meta-predictor shifts toward global. Over many branches this learning produces a per-branch preference that yields higher cumulative accuracy. Understanding this flow is necessary to implement a working tournament in a simulator.

keyIdea.title: Runtime Flow
keyIdea.text: Predictors run in parallel; the selector chooses; after resolution both predictors and the selector are updated based on correctness to learn the preferred source.

content.html:
Process Flow Tournament Runtime
Step-by-step
  1. Fetch: compute local and global predictions in parallel.
  2. Select: meta-predictor chooses which to use for fetch-time speculation.
  3. Resolve: when branch outcome is known, compare each predictor to the real outcome.
  4. Update: update both predictor tables and adjust the meta-predictor toward the more accurate predictor.
Example
If local predicted taken and global predicted not taken, and the branch is actually not taken, the selector shifts toward global. Repeat over time and the selector converges to the better predictor for that branch address.
Pro tip: give the selector hysteresis by using a 2-bit counter so the predictor doesn't flip on a single outcome.

screens.title: Branch Target Buffer (BTB)
screens.narratorSegment: Predicting the branch direction is only half the job; the processor also needs the target address for taken branches so instruction fetch can continue without delay. The Branch Target Buffer, or BTB, is a small cache that stores the target addresses of recently taken branches. Typical BTB entries include an index derived from low PC bits, a tag for higher PC bits, and data such as the target address and often a taken/not-taken prediction bit. When an instruction fetch encounters a PC that matches an entry, the BTB supplies the target immediately and the fetch unit can speculatively start fetching from that address. For PC-relative branches the target can be computed from the offset, but for indirect branches, such as virtual calls or function pointers, the BTB is essential because the target comes from a register and cannot be computed cheaply. BTB sizes vary — designs commonly use 512 to 4096 entries depending on complexity. A misconception is that larger BTBs always help; they reduce misses but increase access latency and power. Index/tag organization matters: low bits index into sets and tags confirm the entry. Knowing how to design and size a BTB is crucial to understanding practical branch-target prediction and its impact on front-end performance.

keyIdea.title: BTB Role
keyIdea.text: BTB caches recently taken branch targets so the fetch unit can speculatively fetch the correct instructions without waiting to compute or load a target.

content.html:
Architecture Branch Target Buffer
BTB entry fields
  • • Index: low bits of PC to select a set or entry.
  • • Tag: high bits of PC to validate the entry.
  • • Data: target address and optional prediction bits.
  • • Size: typically hundreds to a few thousand entries.
Why BTB matters
For indirect branches the BTB supplies a cached target immediately. For taken conditional branches it avoids waiting for target computation, enabling deeper speculative fetch and better pipeline utilization.
Design trade-offs: larger BTBs reduce misses but increase access time and complexity; associativity and tag bits shape collision behavior.
Try this
Measure fetch bubbles with and without a 16-entry BTB on a trace containing indirect calls.

screens.title: Indirect branch prediction and BTB limits
screens.narratorSegment: Indirect branches — such as function pointers, virtual calls, and switch dispatches — are challenging because their target is not encoded as a PC-relative offset but comes from a register or memory value. The BTB can cache recent targets for a given branch PC, but it has limits. If a branch frequently jumps to many different targets, the BTB entry for that PC may thrash, or entries may alias, producing mispredictions. A BTB miss forces the processor to compute or load the target, causing fetch stalls. The common misconception is to assume that caching targets always yields near-perfect coverage; in reality, indirect branches with high target diversity or rare call sites will see many BTB misses. Some processors augment the BTB with a small target history or use separate indirect predictors, but the basic point is that BTB capacity shapes how well indirect branches are predicted. Concrete scenario: a virtual function call site that dispatches to multiple derived classes will produce many different targets; a small BTB of 16 entries may only capture the hot targets and miss the rest. When designing or simulating, measure BTB hit rates on your workload and consider whether a larger BTB or more sophisticated indirect-target mechanism is justified by the accuracy gains.

keyIdea.title: Indirect Branches
keyIdea.text: Indirect targets are hard to predict; BTBs help but can miss when target diversity or aliasing exceeds their capacity.

content.html:
Definition Indirect Branches & BTB Limits
Why indirects are tricky
  • • Target comes from a register or memory, not a PC-relative offset.
  • • Many possible targets lead to BTB thrash and increased misses.
  • • BTB misses cause fetch delays since the target must be resolved.
Practical scenario
A virtual dispatch site with many derived classes produces diversified targets. A small BTB will capture only the hottest targets and will miss on less-common ones, increasing misprediction penalties.
Measure: track BTB hit rate per indirect branch and inspect the distribution of targets to decide if a larger BTB or specialized indirect predictor is warranted.

screens.title: Return Address Stack (RAS)
screens.narratorSegment: Function returns are highly structured: a call instruction pushes a return address and the corresponding return should return to that same address. The return address stack, or RAS, exploits this structure by pushing the return address on a small hardware stack at call time and popping it on return. This gives near-perfect prediction for nested calls because the RAS mirrors the call/return nesting. Typical RAS sizes are 8 to 32 entries. However, the RAS is limited: deeply nested recursive calls that exceed the RAS capacity overflow the stack and cause mispredictions. Implementations often use a circular buffer to reduce overflow harm, but correctness requires careful handling when the static call/return structure is interrupted by exceptions, context switches, or nonstandard call/return sequences. A common misconception is that RAS is unnecessary because the BTB can store return targets; in practice the RAS is far cheaper and more accurate for well-nested call/return patterns. A concrete example: a sequence of nested function calls of depth 12 will be predicted correctly by a 16-entry RAS; but a recursive algorithm with depth 100 will overflow and mispredict beyond the RAS capacity. The takeaway is that RAS gives near-perfect returns for typical code but has explicit capacity limits that designers must respect.

keyIdea.title: RAS Role
keyIdea.text: RAS predicts return addresses by pushing on call and popping on return; it gives excellent accuracy for nested calls but is limited by stack depth.

content.html:
Definition Return Address Stack
How RAS works
On a call, push return address; on a return, pop the predicted return address and use it to speculatively fetch the caller's next instruction.
Common limitation: hardware stack overflow on deeply nested calls. Circular buffers help but cannot make the RAS infinite.
Concrete example
A 16-entry RAS handles typical call nesting in most programs. A recursive routine that goes deeper than 16 will overflow and start mispredicting returns until the stack unwinds.
Key Takeaway

RAS is a low-cost, high-accuracy mechanism for call/return prediction but must be sized for expected nesting depth.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: implement and compare predictors
screens.narratorSegment: This lab extends your simulator from the previous chapter. The three tasks are: first, add a gshare predictor with an 8-bit GHR and a 256-entry 2-bit counter table; second, implement a tournament predictor composed of a local 2-bit predictor, a gshare global predictor, and a 2-bit meta-predictor, each with 256 entries; third, add a simple BTB with 16 entries to cache targets. Start by implementing the GHR shift and the XOR index for gshare. Test on a trace with correlated branches such as the three-branch example where Branch 3 depends on Branches 1 and 2. Measure accuracy and compare to a baseline per-branch 2-bit predictor. Next, implement local and global tables and a meta-table that selects which to use for each branch PC index. Ensure your simulator updates both predictors and the meta-predictor on branch resolution. Finally, add a BTB: index by low PC bits, store tag and target, and measure BTB hit rate on indirect branches. A common mistake is updating the GHR at the wrong time; update it on actual resolution, not speculation, to keep training correct. After implementation, produce accuracy numbers for each predictor and a short chart comparing them. Reflect: how many percentage points did tournament add over gshare and the simple 2-bit predictor on your trace?

keyIdea.title: Lab Goal
keyIdea.text: Implement gshare, a tournament predictor, and a 16-entry BTB; measure and compare their accuracies on correlated traces.

content.html:
Lab Walkthrough Implement & Compare
Step 1 — gshare
Add an 8-bit GHR and a 256-entry 2-bit table. Compute index = (PC_low8 ^ GHR) & 0xFF. Update counter_table[index] on resolution and shift the real outcome into GHR.
Step 2 — tournament
Add a local 256-entry 2-bit table indexed by PC_low8, a gshare global table (256 entries), and a meta 256-entry 2-bit selector. On resolution update local, global, and meta based on correctness.
Step 3 — BTB
Implement a 16-entry BTB with index = PC_low4, store tag and target. Report BTB hit rate and effect on fetch stalls for indirect branches.
Experiment
Run traces with correlated branches and report accuracy for: 2-bit baseline, gshare, tournament. Note how meta-predictor behavior changes per branch.
Starter pseudocode
// update gshare
index = (PC_low << 0) ^ GHR
if (outcome == TAKEN) counter[index] = min(counter[index]+1, 3) else counter[index] = max(counter[index]-1, 0)
GHR = ((GHR << 1) | (outcome==TAKEN?1:0)) & 0xFF

// meta update
if (global_correct && !local_correct) meta[index] = min(meta[index]+1,3)
if (local_correct && !global_correct) meta[index] = max(meta[index]-1,0)

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate the essential ideas. First, the GHR records recent branch outcomes and provides the context that correlation-based predictors use to distinguish execution patterns. Second, gshare mixes PC bits with GHR via XOR to index a 2-bit counter table, reducing some aliasing and improving accuracy for correlated branches. Third, tournament predictors run local and global predictors in parallel and use a meta-predictor to select the better predictor per branch over time. Also remember the supporting hardware: the BTB caches branch targets for quicker speculative fetch, and the RAS pushes and pops return addresses to predict function returns with high reliability. Be aware of trade-offs: history length, table sizes, and selector hysteresis all influence accuracy and cost. Finally, implementing these structures in a simulator and measuring accuracy on correlated traces is the best way to internalize how they interact. What small experiment will you run first to see gshare's effect in your simulator?

What to Remember
Global History (GHR)
Records recent branch outcomes to provide context for correlated predictions.
Gshare
Index = PC XOR GHR; uses 2-bit counters to capture patterns conditioned on recent history.
Tournament
Combine local and global predictors with a meta-selector that learns per branch.
Summary: GHR, table design, selector behavior, BTB and RAS sizing are the levers you can tune to improve accuracy versus cost.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.narratorSegment: A final quick reference: first, global history is context — pick an N that balances pattern depth and hardware cost. Second, combining predictors works: gshare reduces harmful aliasing by mixing PC bits with history, and a tournament selector adapts to different branch behaviors. Third, target prediction and return prediction complete performance improvements: the BTB supplies targets to avoid fetch stalls and the RAS provides highly accurate return predictions for nested calls. Keep these three in mind as you design, implement, or evaluate branch predictors. For practice, instrument your simulator to report prediction accuracy, BTB hit rate, and RAS overflows — those metrics tell the story of whether your design choices help on real traces. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means tune ghr size, use xor indexing for gshare, combine predictors with a meta-selector, and size btb/ras for your workload.. In practical terms, three compact reminders to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore how branch prediction moves beyond independent two-bit counters to use correlations, selectors, and small caches so a processor can guess both whether a branch is taken and where it goes. You will learn what a global branch history register records, how the gshare predictor mixes that history with a branch address to index a table, and why tournament predictors combine a local and a global view with a meta-predictor to pick the best source of truth. We also cover the branch target buffer, which supplies destination addresses for taken branches, and the return address stack, which restores return addresses for nested calls. These pieces are practical engineering: gshare and tournament designs appear in real processors because correlated behavior and call/return patterns provide consistent signals that simple per-branch counters miss. By the end you will understand the key trade-offs — accuracy versus aliasing and hardware cost — and you will be ready to extend a branch-prediction simulator to implement gshare, a tournament selector, and a small BTB. Think about a detective who uses a notebook of recent cases: that notebook is the global history that helps make smarter local decisions.

By the end of these lessons you will explain how global branch history improves prediction and implement a gshare predictor in a simulator. You will also describe tournament predictors that combine local and global predictions and explain the role of the BTB and RAS in supplying targets and return addresses. Each objective maps to a measurable competency: explain, implement, describe, and understand. For example, when asked about gshare you should be able to show how the GHR bits are XORed with bits of the program counter to produce an index into a 2-bit counter table and argue why that reduces aliasing for correlated branches. When asked about tournament predictors you should explain how a meta-predictor tracks which predictor was more accurate and switches accordingly. For the BTB and RAS you should describe how they reduce pipeline stalls by enabling speculative fetch of branch targets and return addresses. We'll also give a short hands-on lab so you can implement these structures and measure accuracy improvements on traces with correlated branches.

In this applied view we'll connect each objective to a concrete task so you can show mastery. First, explaining global history means you should be able to read an N-bit GHR like 10110101 and explain why those bits form context for the next branch. A worked example might show how a branch's probability changes when prior bits differ. Second, implementing gshare means modifying a simulator: compute an index by XORing PC bits with the GHR and update 2-bit saturating counters; then report accuracy on a trace with correlated branches. Third, describing tournaments is shown by building a selector table that chooses local or global prediction per branch and by demonstrating the selector learning over time. Finally, understanding BTB and RAS is demonstrated by instrumenting a small BTB to supply speculative targets and a RAS to push/pop return addresses during call/return sequences. Each of these applied tasks is small but revealing — they show how context, selection, and cached targets combine to raise prediction accuracy in real hardware.

A simple two-bit saturating counter treats each branch as independent, which works well for some patterns but fails when branches are correlated. Define correlation here as a statistical dependence: the outcome of branch B changes depending on whether a previous branch A was taken. For example, consider code where a second comparison only runs after the first test passes. A 2-bit counter for branch B averages all outcomes it sees and may settle on the majority behavior, losing the conditional nuance. That leads to predictable mistakes when B behaves differently in the two contexts. A concrete case is Branch B taken 90 percent of the time when Branch A was taken but only 30 percent when Branch A was not taken. The 2-bit predictor may converge near 60 percent and mispredict frequently in both contexts. The misconception learners often have is thinking more bits solve correlation; adding bits to a per-branch counter doesn't add context about other branches. The correct remedy is to add history: a register that records recent outcomes, so the predictor can index different table entries per context. The takeaway is simple: independence assumptions are cheap but lose accuracy when program flow carries contextual signals that connect branches.

The global branch history register, or GHR, is a compact shift register that records the taken/not-taken outcomes of the most recent N branches. Each bit is 1 for taken and 0 for not taken, so an 8-bit GHR might read 10110101 and represent the last eight outcomes in order. The GHR provides temporal context for the next branch: patterns of recent branches often repeat across program behavior, and these patterns can strongly influence a later branch. A key practical detail is which branches contribute bits — typically all conditional branches update the GHR in fetch or retire stages. A common misconception is that longer GHRs always improve accuracy. Longer history captures longer patterns but increases table aliasing and hardware cost, and older bits might be irrelevant for the current decision. Balance is required: small GHRs capture local correlations with lower aliasing risk. An example: a conditional inside a sequence of checks can be predicted more accurately when the GHR preserves the outcomes of those checks. In practice, the GHR is the contextual notebook the predictor consults before making a decision; understanding what it records and how long it should be is the first step to building correlation-based predictors.

Gshare mixes global history with branch-specific information by XORing bits of the program counter with the GHR to produce an index into a table of 2-bit saturating counters. This simple operation distributes contexts so different branches with the same history do not always alias to the same entry. The formula is: Index = (PC XOR GHR) mod TableSize. Practically, implementations often use the lower bits of the PC and the low-order bits of the GHR for the XOR. A common implementation detail is to mask to the table size using bitwise AND when the table size is a power of two. For example, with an 8-bit GHR and a 256-entry table, XOR the low 8 bits of PC with the GHR to get an 8-bit index. A misconception is thinking XOR always eliminates aliasing; XOR reduces some alias patterns but does not remove aliasing entirely. Concrete example: suppose the GHR is 0b11001010 and the PC low bits are 0b10101010; XOR yields 0b01100000 which is used to select a saturating counter. In a simulator, implement this index computation in fetch or prediction stage, update the counter on branch resolution, and update the GHR by shifting in the actual outcome. The result: gshare often raises accuracy for branches whose outcomes depend on recent history.

Correlation-based predictors come in multiple flavors and each makes different trade-offs between per-branch specificity and global sharing. PAg uses a per-branch history register for each dynamic branch and then a shared global pattern table that maps those per-branch histories to predictions. That gives per-branch context while still sharing a global prediction table. GAg uses a single global history register and a single global pattern table shared by all branches; it captures global correlations but is more prone to aliasing since unrelated branches map into the same table patterns. The core trade-off is specificity versus sharing: PAg gives more specificity for heavy branches at the cost of more storage for per-branch history, while GAg is simpler and cheaper but can suffer when many branches collide in the same entries. A frequent misconception is that per-branch histories eliminate aliasing; they reduce aliasing for that branch but the global pattern table can still collide entries from different branches. A concrete example: a hot loop branch benefits from a dedicated per-branch history because its short repeating pattern maps cleanly to different pattern table entries than other code. When designing a predictor, measure aliasing and storage cost against accuracy to choose the right balance for your target workload.

A tournament predictor runs two or more predictors in parallel, typically a local predictor that relies on the branch address and a global predictor that uses GHR, and then uses a meta-predictor or selector to choose which prediction to trust for each branch. The meta-predictor is often implemented as a 2-bit counter per branch index that increments when the global predictor succeeds and decrements when the local predictor succeeds, or vice versa. Over time it favors the predictor that has been more accurate for that branch. This design addresses the central practical observation: different branches have different predictability characteristics — some are best solved by local repetition, others by global correlations. The trade-off is extra hardware: two prediction tables plus the meta-selector. The value shows up in real workloads: tournaments can reach high accuracy because they adapt to branch behavior at the granularity of branch addresses. A concrete example: a loop counter is best handled by a local predictor, while a conditional dependent on a prior branch benefits from the global predictor; the meta-predictor learns which to use. A common misconception is that the meta-predictor instantly switches; in reality it learns gradually from outcomes and can be conservative to avoid thrashing. The takeaway: tournament predictors adaptively pick the right model for each branch and are a key building block of modern high-accuracy predictors.

At runtime a tournament predictor predicts by running local and global predictors in parallel and using the meta-predictor to pick one result. The process starts at fetch: both predictors compute their choices based on the branch address and the GHR. The meta-predictor provides a selector value that determines which prediction to send to the fetch pipeline. Speculation proceeds; when the branch resolves in execute or retire, the predictor logic compares each predictor's guess to the actual outcome. The meta-predictor is updated: if the chosen predictor was correct and the other was incorrect, the selector is biased toward the chosen predictor; if the other predictor was correct, the selector is adjusted in the opposite direction. The predictors' own tables are updated as usual. A common misconception is thinking the meta-predictor only toggles when the chosen predictor fails; in fact it considers both predictors' correctness and adjusts slowly to avoid oscillation on noisy branches. Concrete example: local predicted taken, global predicted not-taken, actual outcome not-taken — the meta-predictor shifts toward global. Over many branches this learning produces a per-branch preference that yields higher cumulative accuracy. Understanding this flow is necessary to implement a working tournament in a simulator.

Predicting the branch direction is only half the job; the processor also needs the target address for taken branches so instruction fetch can continue without delay. The Branch Target Buffer, or BTB, is a small cache that stores the target addresses of recently taken branches. Typical BTB entries include an index derived from low PC bits, a tag for higher PC bits, and data such as the target address and often a taken/not-taken prediction bit. When an instruction fetch encounters a PC that matches an entry, the BTB supplies the target immediately and the fetch unit can speculatively start fetching from that address. For PC-relative branches the target can be computed from the offset, but for indirect branches, such as virtual calls or function pointers, the BTB is essential because the target comes from a register and cannot be computed cheaply. BTB sizes vary — designs commonly use 512 to 4096 entries depending on complexity. A misconception is that larger BTBs always help; they reduce misses but increase access latency and power. Index/tag organization matters: low bits index into sets and tags confirm the entry. Knowing how to design and size a BTB is crucial to understanding practical branch-target prediction and its impact on front-end performance.

Indirect branches — such as function pointers, virtual calls, and switch dispatches — are challenging because their target is not encoded as a PC-relative offset but comes from a register or memory value. The BTB can cache recent targets for a given branch PC, but it has limits. If a branch frequently jumps to many different targets, the BTB entry for that PC may thrash, or entries may alias, producing mispredictions. A BTB miss forces the processor to compute or load the target, causing fetch stalls. When designing or simulating, measure BTB hit rates on your workload and consider whether a larger BTB or more sophisticated indirect-target mechanism is justified by the accuracy gains.

Function returns are highly structured: a call instruction pushes a return address and the corresponding return should return to that same address. The return address stack, or RAS, exploits this structure by pushing the return address on a small hardware stack at call time and popping it on return. However, the RAS is limited: deeply nested recursive calls that exceed the RAS capacity overflow the stack and cause mispredictions. Implementations often use a circular buffer to reduce overflow harm, but correctness requires careful handling when the static call/return structure is interrupted by exceptions, context switches, or nonstandard call/return sequences. A common misconception is that RAS is unnecessary because the BTB can store return targets; in practice the RAS is far cheaper and more accurate for well-nested call/return patterns. A concrete example: a sequence of nested function calls of depth 12 will be predicted correctly by a 16-entry RAS; but a recursive algorithm with depth 100 will overflow and mispredict beyond the RAS capacity. The takeaway is that RAS gives near-perfect returns for typical code but has explicit capacity limits that designers must respect.
